name: Radius Residential Care Limited
overview: Radius Residential Care is a New Zealand aged residential care operator focused on higher-acuity hospital-level, dementia, psychogeriatric, ACC and respite care, operating 25 care homes and four retirement villages with over 2,000 beds as at the FY2026 (year ended 31 March 2026) balance date. Unlike the large listed retirement-village groups, Radius is a care-only operator layering on adjacent services (Cibus catering, Home Support, Luma continence products, Radius Shop) rather than an integrated care-plus-village-unit developer, and funds its growth through a mix of owned freehold property and third-party-financed leasehold care homes. It listed on the NZX in 2021 and remains founder-led, with Executive Chair Brien Cree and related entities holding a significant shareholding.

business_model.summary: Revenue is overwhelmingly government-funded aged-care bed-days (rest home, hospital and dementia fees plus accommodation supplements paid by Health New Zealand, WINZ and ACC), supplemented by resident-funded premium/extra services, village service fees on a small owned retirement-village base, and a growing slice of ancillary/adjacent revenue (Cibus catering, Home Support, Radius Shop, Luma). Approximately half of the 25-home portfolio is leased from third-party (including related-party) property owners rather than owned outright by Radius, which keeps balance-sheet capital intensity lower but creates a large IFRS-16 lease liability ($141.5m at FY2026, versus $71.6m of bank borrowings) and a structural rent/lease cost that sits above EBITDA. Radius's target capital framework is to keep 25%-50% of the portfolio owned freehold, funding the balance via a 'capital-light' new-build model backed by long-term private property investors -- new care homes are typically financed and owned by third parties and leased back to Radius on long terms (e.g., 30-year initial lease with two 10-year rights of renewal on the FY26 St Allisa sale-and-leaseback).

revenue_streams.name: Rest home, hospital and dementia care fees (govt-funded bed-day rate)
Village service fees / other care revenue / rental income
Other services (Home Support, Radius Shop, Luma)

business_model.customer_type: Government-funded (Health New Zealand, Work and Income New Zealand, ACC) as the primary payer on behalf of residents, supplemented by privately-paying residents for premium rooms/services and ACC/private clients for Home Support; effectively a B2G/B2C hybrid with a single dominant payer for the bulk of revenue
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand; 25 care homes and 4 villages spread nationally, newly expanded into Wellington (Karori, first Wellington home, from May 2026) and planned expansion to the West Coast (Hokitika)

main_competitors: numerous independent/charitable rest-home and hospital operators
competitive_position.market_position: Smallest of the NZX-listed aged-care/retirement operators and structurally different in model: Radius is care-only (hospital, dementia, rest-home) with only 2 small legacy retirement villages, versus SUM/RYM/OCA/ARV which are primarily integrated retirement-village developers (large-format ORA/DMF-funded independent-living and serviced-apartment portfolios with care centres attached). Radius reports sector-leading EBITDAR per occupied care bed (~$31k in FY26, +11% YoY) and above-average occupancy (94.9%), reflecting a deliberate focus on higher-acuity, harder-to-serve care categories that face less price competition than standard rest-home beds.

moat_factors.description: Aged residential care requires certification/licensing and significant construction/consenting lead times, and NZ faces a structural bed shortfall (Ministry-modelled shortfall of over 9,000 residential beds by the late 2030s), which supports pricing and occupancy for existing operators, but barriers do not stop the large well-capitalised village developers from competing for the same government funding pool

Deep focus on hospital-level, dementia and psychogeriatric care (harder to deliver, lower staff turnover at 18%, strong resident satisfaction/NPS) differentiates Radius from operators chasing lower-acuity, ORA-fee-driven village growth

Growth funded by private property investors taking on development/leasehold risk lets Radius add beds without the balance-sheet intensity of SUM/RYM/OCA, though this trades moat strength for financial leverage (see risks)

Aged care admission decisions are largely need- and location-driven rather than brand-driven; switching costs for residents are low pre-admission (high post-admission for the resident, but that does not create pricing power over the government payer)
At ~2,000 beds Radius is materially smaller than the big-six village operators, which limits procurement, workforce and back-office scale economies relative to SUM/RYM/OCA/ARV

weaknesses: Single dominant payer (Health New Zealand/government subsidy) sets the bed-day rate, making Radius a price-taker with limited ability to pass through wage and cost inflation outside of scheduled funding reviews

Leasehold-heavy portfolio (roughly half of care homes leased, including from related parties) creates a large, growing lease liability and rent/interest cost load that a fully-owned operator like Ryman or Summerset does not carry to the same degree
No village/ORA scale to speak of relative to peers, so Radius largely forgoes the deferred-management-fee/capital-gain economics that underpin SUM/RYM/OCA/ARV's retirement-village earnings model
Small-cap NZX illiquidity limits institutional ownership and can produce outsized share-price moves on results
Related-party transactions (sale-and-leaseback with a common-shareholder entity, consulting/legal fees to director-related firms) require ongoing governance scrutiny even though disclosed and audited

growth_drivers: New Zealand demographic ageing tailwind: population aged 65+ projected to grow from ~950,000 to ~1.3 million by 2040, with a Ministerial Advisory Group-modelled national shortfall of 9,000+ residential care beds by the late 2030s absent intervention

Potential funding-rate uplift: the August 2026 Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group report recommended the government commit to 'significant price uplifts,' including a modelled ~7.1% increase in residential care per-bed pricing and lowering the asset threshold for means-tested contributions -- a material tailwind if legislated, though not yet committed government policy
Occupancy recovery/optimisation: average occupancy of 94.9% in FY26 (up 2.1pp YoY), with management targeting 97-98% over time, against a higher-acuity, higher-turnover bed mix

Disciplined, capital-light new-build and brownfield/greenfield development pipeline: ~20 new 80-100 bed care homes targeted over the coming years, funded by private property investors, plus adjacent village development (e.g., Christchurch Applefields, Hokitika, Matamata, Invercargill, Karori)

Bolt-on M&A: recent acquisitions of St Allisa (109 beds, May 2025) and Karori Village (90 beds, Wellington's first Radius home, settled late May 2026), with further acquisitions continue to be assessed as they arise

Diversification into adjacent, less government-payer-dependent revenue: Cibus Catering (external site growth), Home Support (ACC Maximise Independence accreditation), Luma continence products and Radius Shop, aimed at capturing more of the ageing/care value chain and reducing single-payer concentration over time

business.description: The large majority of revenue derives from Health New Zealand, WINZ and ACC-set subsidy rates; any funding freeze, delay or unfavourable rate-setting materially compresses margins given largely fixed cost structures

Employee costs rose from $106.3m to $123.0m (+16%) in FY26, faster than revenue in absolute terms; the sector faces a widely-recognised workforce shortage and reliance on the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme for migrant care workers, with minimum wage increases (to NZ$23.95/hour from April 2026) and tightening AEWV language/eligibility requirements adding cost and hiring friction

business.risk: Occupancy risk in a high-acuity model
business.description: Higher-acuity residents have shorter, more frequent stays (admissions/discharges), making occupancy inherently harder to sustain than in standard low-acuity rest-home or independent-living settings

business.risk: Small scale versus larger integrated peers
business.description: Limited procurement and back-office scale relative to Summerset, Ryman, Oceania and Arvida, and no meaningful ORA/village capital-gain earnings stream to offset care-margin pressure

financial.description: Total lease liabilities of $141.5m plus bank borrowings of $71.6m against net assets of $76.3m as at 31 March 2026; net debt (bank facility basis) of $68.7m, up 1% YoY, with a medium-term target of Net Bank Debt/EBITDA below 2.5x. Interest rate risk is partially hedged (49% of interest-bearing borrowings under swaps) but a 100bp rate move still affects profit after tax by ~$0.5m

financial.risk: Bank covenant risk (monitored, not currently breached)
financial.description: ASB Bank facilities ($88.0m total commitment, extended/reorganised June 2025 to expire mostly June 2028) carry quarterly-tested fixed charge cover, leverage and equity ratio covenants; the FY2026 annual report explicitly states the Group complied with all covenants during the period and as at year end, and management's forecast supports continued compliance for at least the next 12 months with no material risk of the non-current borrowings becoming repayable -- there is no going-concern qualification or material uncertainty paragraph in the FY2026 audit opinion (clean, unqualified opinion), but the leveraged, leasehold-heavy structure means this remains a metric worth monitoring each period

Land and buildings for the FY26 St Allisa acquisition were sold and immediately leased back to a related party (Warehouse Storage Limited, common shareholder), and other related-party consulting/legal/rent arrangements exist; while disclosed, audited and flagged as a Key Audit Matter, this concentrates counterparty and terms risk with insiders

regulatory.description: The August 2026 Ministerial Advisory Group report recommends structural changes (means-testing threshold cuts, integrated funding models); while the headline recommendation (a ~7.1% price uplift) is a potential positive, any reform is subject to government decision and Budget appropriation, and structural changes could alter competitive dynamics or shift funding toward home-based care over residential beds

Aged care is heavily reliant on the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme; tightening English-language and other AEWV requirements from mid-2026, absent a clear national aged-care workforce strategy (a gap flagged by the NZ Aged Care Association), adds hiring cost and risk

Four-year facility certification is the sector benchmark; Radius reports a strong compliance record (3 of 4 audited homes achieved maximum four-year certification in FY26), but any decline in clinical/audit outcomes could trigger funding or reputational consequences

macro.description: Bank debt (weighted average 5.31% at FY26, down from ~7.4% at FY25 as rates eased) and lease liabilities (discounted at ~5.1%) mean the business benefits from falling NZ rates and is exposed if rates rise again; financing costs fell 21% YoY in H1 FY26 on lower rates

The development pipeline (new-build 80-100 bed homes, villa construction) is exposed to NZ construction cost and contractor availability cycles, which affects the economics of both Radius's owned development and its private-investor-funded leasehold pipeline
NZX small-cap (~NZ$127m market cap) with limited daily liquidity and founder/related-party concentration in the share register, which can amplify volatility and limit institutional participation

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Structurally favourable long-term demand backdrop (NZ 65+ population growing from ~950,000 to ~1.3 million by 2040) colliding with a supply-constrained, government-price-capped sector; the August 2026 Ministerial Advisory Group report explicitly warns current settings cannot meet future demand without major reform and models a 9,000+ bed shortfall by the late 2030s absent intervention, which is a broadly positive backdrop for well-run incumbent operators, but funding adequacy remains politically and fiscally contingent
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate — aged-care demand is largely non-discretionary and demographically driven rather than tied to the economic cycle, but funding-rate settings are subject to Budget cycles and government fiscal constraints, and development/M&A activity is exposed to construction and credit cycles
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high given ~$213m of combined lease liabilities and bank borrowings at FY26; falling NZ interest rates were a tailwind in FY26 (finance costs fell materially), and further RBNZ rate movements will flow through both bank facility and (to a lesser extent, given largely fixed lease discount rates) lease interest expense
key_input_costs: Registered nurse and care-worker wages (incl. minimum wage and pay equity settings)
Construction/build costs for new care homes and villages
Property lease/rent costs on the ~half of the portfolio that is leasehold
Food and catering input costs (via Cibus)

recent_developments.event: Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group released its report ('A place to grow old'), recommending significant residential-care price uplifts (~7.1% modelled), a lower means-testing asset threshold, and structural funding reform; Executive Chair Brien Cree sits on this Ministerial Advisory Group
Radius settled the acquisition of Karori Village (90 beds), its first care home in Wellington, taking the portfolio to 25 care homes and over 2,000 beds

FY2026 (year ended 31 March 2026) results released: revenue $202.3m (+14%), profit before tax $14.3m (+37%), NPAT $9.5m (+34% attributable to owners), Underlying EBITDA $27.4m (+17%), Underlying EBITDAR per bed $31.1k (+11%), AFFO $12.7m (+44%), average occupancy 94.9% (+2.1pp); final dividend raised 50% to 1.20 cps fully imputed

Acquired ~4.3 hectares of development land in Belfast, Christchurch, for the first newly-designed 100-bed care home plus an adjacent ~75-79 villa retirement village, drawing $5.5m from a new bank facility (Facility C) to fund it

H1 FY2026 (six months to 30 September 2025) results: NPAT $6.3m (+221% YoY), Underlying EBITDA $14.9m (+41%), total revenue $100.2m (+17%), interim dividend raised 54% to 1.0 cps, net debt down 6% to $63.7m

Reorganised and extended ASB Bank committed facilities (consolidating and refinancing prior facilities, adding a new development facility), extending most maturities to 15 June 2028 and improving the funding base ahead of the growth pipeline

Acquired the St Allisa dementia/rest-home/hospital care home (109 beds) in Christchurch for $14.6m, concurrently entering a sale-and-leaseback of the land and buildings with a related party (Warehouse Storage Limited) for $13.6m on a 30-year initial lease term

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Results / Investor Presentation, 13 May 2026

items.target: Continued growth in key financial metrics
items.notes: Management guided qualitatively to growth in key financial metrics versus FY26 ($202.3m revenue, $27.4m Underlying EBITDA); no specific numeric FY27 revenue or EBITDA range was disclosed in the annual report
FY26 average occupancy was 94.9% (up from 92.9%); management flagged the higher-acuity bed mix makes very high occupancy harder to sustain due to more frequent admissions/discharges
Formal capital management framework target; net bank debt was $68.7m at FY26 (up 1% YoY)

items.target: 25%-50% of total care home portfolio owned freehold
items.notes: Formal capital management framework target balancing capital-light leasehold growth against owned-asset resilience

items.vs_prior: maintained; FY26 actual payout was 49% of AFFO
items.notes: FY26 total cash dividends were 2.2 cps (gross yield 8.0%); final dividend of 1.20 cps declared 13 May 2026, paid 11 June 2026

items.target: ~20 new 80-100 bed care homes over the next few years (target run-rate of roughly one new home per quarter once ramped)
items.notes: Capital-light model backed by long-term private property investors; first two sites (Applefields, Christchurch and Hokitika) have commenced earthworks; management stated no acquisitions are currently budgeted beyond the organic pipeline
Disclosed capital commitments at year end; excludes the subsequent $13.6m Karori acquisition (settled 26 May 2026) and Belfast land development spend

guidance.management_commentary: Executive Chair Brien Cree and CEO Andrew Peskett characterised FY26 as reflecting 'the strength of our focus on care and the disciplined execution of our growth strategy,' citing stronger occupancy, improved care mix, continued accommodation-supplement growth, disciplined cost management and lower financing costs. Management emphasised a 'disciplined growth' posture -- prioritising quality of care over speed of bed additions -- and flagged that near-term growth will be led by new-builds under the capital-light, private-investor-funded model rather than large M&A, while continuing to selectively pursue acquisitions and adjacent-service expansion (Home Support, Luma, Radius Shop, complementary health services) as it arises.

bull_case: Structural, non-discretionary demand tailwind from NZ's ageing population and a government-modelled national bed shortfall, with the August 2026 Ministerial Advisory Group explicitly recommending significant residential-care funding uplifts (~7.1% modelled) that would flow straight to Radius's largely fixed-cost care margins if adopted

Momentum in the numbers: FY26 revenue +14%, PBT +37%, NPAT +34%, AFFO +44%, occupancy up 2.1pp to 94.9%, and H1 FY27-adjacent commentary of continued growth, alongside a 50% dividend increase and an 8.0% gross yield at recent prices

Sector-leading EBITDAR per occupied bed (~$31k, +11% YoY) evidencing a differentiated, higher-acuity clinical focus that is harder for lower-cost competitors to replicate and commands funding-partner and referrer trust (NPS +40, 91% resident satisfaction)

Disciplined, capital-light growth model (private-investor-funded new-builds plus bolt-on acquisitions like St Allisa and Karori) that can scale bed count without proportionate balance-sheet strain, while refinanced ASB facilities extend runway to mid-2028
Diversification optionality (Cibus, Home Support, Luma, Radius Shop) gradually reduces dependence on the single government payer and adds higher-margin, less-regulated revenue streams
bear_case: Single-payer concentration leaves Radius a price-taker: absent legislated funding uplifts (not yet committed government policy despite the Advisory Group's recommendation), wage and cost inflation can outpace the government-set bed-day rate and compress margins, as seen with FY26 employee costs (+16%) growing faster than revenue mix would ideally support

Elevated leverage and lease load for a small-cap operator -- $141.5m of lease liabilities plus $71.6m of bank borrowings against $76.3m of net assets -- means covenant compliance (currently satisfied, per the clean FY26 audit opinion) needs to be monitored every reporting period as the leasehold-heavy, capital-light growth model keeps adding to both sides of the balance sheet

Persistent aged-care workforce shortage and tightening immigration settings (AEWV language/eligibility changes, rising minimum wage) could constrain the ability to staff new beds or push labour costs higher without an offsetting funding response

Structurally thin moat versus the larger, better-capitalised village operators (Summerset, Ryman, Oceania, Arvida), who can cross-subsidise care margins with ORA/DMF village economics that Radius largely lacks, and who have far greater scale to absorb funding-rate shortfalls

Small-cap NZX illiquidity and a founder/related-party-concentrated share register (including a related-party sale-and-leaseback structure) add governance and liquidity risk premia that could cap re-rating even if operating performance continues to improve
